title: The dialogue of Jason and Papiscus
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις ἐπιλεξάμενος ἀπὸ πάντων συγγραμμάτων. τῶν περιεχόντων ἀλληγορίας καὶ διηγήσεις μετὰ οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτου λέξεως, τὸ εὐτελέστερον καὶ δυνάμενον μέν τι πρὸς τοὺς πολλοὺς καὶ ἁπλουστέρους πίστεως χάριν συμβαλέσθαι οὐ μὴν οἷόν τε καὶ τοὺς συνετωτέρους κινῆσαι, φησίν· οἵαν δὴ καὶ Παπίσκου τινὸς καὶ Ἰάσονος ἀντιλογίαν ἔγνων, οὐ γέλωτος ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐλέους καὶ μίσους ἀξίαν. ἔμοιγ᾿ οὖν οὐ ταῦτ᾿ ἐλέγχειν πρόκειται· ἔστι γὰρ παντί που δῆλα, καὶ μάλιστα εἴ τις ὑπομείναι καὶ ἀνάσχοιτο αὐτῶν ἐπακοῦσαι τῶν συγγραμμάτων. ἀλλ᾿ ἐκεῖνο μᾶλλον ἐθέλω διδάξαι τὴν φύσιν, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς οὐδὲν θνητὸν ἐποίησεν· ἀλλὰ θεοῦ μὲν ἔργα ὅσα ἀθάνατα. θνητὰ δ᾿ ἐκείνων. καὶ ψυχὴ μὲν θεοῦ ἔργον, σώματος δὲ ἄλλη φύσις. καὶ ταύτῃ γε οὐδὲν διοίσει νυκτερίδος ἢ εὐλῆς ἢ βατράχου ἢ ἀνθρώπου σῶμα· ὕλη γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ. καὶ τὸ φθαρτὸν αὐτῶν ὅμοιον. οὐδὲν δ᾿ ἧττον ἐβουλόμην πάνθ᾿ ὁντινοῦν. ἀκούσαντα δεινολογοῦντος Κέλσου καὶ φάσκοντος τὸ ἐπιγεγραμμένον σύγγραμμα Ἰάσονος καὶ Παπίσκου ἀντιλογίαν περὶ Χριστοῦ οὐ γέλωτος ἀλλὰ μίσους ἄξιον εἶναι, λαβεῖν εἰς χεῖρας τὸ συγγραμμάτιον καὶ ὑπομεῖναι καὶ ἀνασχέσθαι ἀκοῦσαι τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ, ἵν᾿ αὐτόθεν καταγνῶ τοῦ Κέλσου, μηδὲν εὑρίσκων μίσους ἄξιον ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ. ἐὰν δ᾿ ἀδεκάστως τις ἐντυγχάνῃ. εὑρήσει ὅτι οὐδ᾿ ἐπὶ γέλωτα κινεῖ τὸ βιβλίον. ἐν ᾧ ἀναγέγραπται Χριστιανὸς Ἰουδαίῳ διαλεγόμενος ἀπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαϊκῶν γραφῶν καὶ δεικνὺς τὰς περὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ προφητείας ἐφαρμόζειν τῷ Ἰησοῦ, καίτοι γε οὐκ ἀγεννῶς οὐδ᾿ ἀπρεπῶς τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ ἑτέρου ἱσταμένου πρὸς τὸν λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: Next after these, having picked out (ἐπιλέγομαι) from all the writings containing allegories and narratives (διήγησις) with a not contemptible (εὐκαταφρόνητος) diction (λέξις) the cheaper (εὐτελέστερον), able to contribute (συμβάλλομαι) something to the many and simpler for the sake of faith (πίστις), but not able to move the more intelligent (συνετός), he says: 'such indeed I knew a certain disputation (ἀντιλογία) of Papiscus and Jason, worthy not of laughter (γέλως) but rather of pity (ἔλεος) and hatred (μῖσος). To me then it is not proposed (πρόκειμαι) to refute (ἐλέγχω) these; for they are plain to everyone, I suppose (που), especially if one should endure (ὑπομένω) and bear (ἀνέχομαι) to listen to the writings themselves. But rather I wish to teach the nature (φύσις): that God made nothing mortal (θνητός), but works of God are whatever are immortal (ἀθάνατος), mortal things of those. And soul (ψυχή) is God's work, but of body (σῶμα) another nature. And in this the body of a bat (νυκτερίς) or maggot (εὐλή) or frog (βάτραχος) or man will differ nothing; for the matter (ὕλη) is the same, and their perishable (φθαρτός) part alike.' Nonetheless I would wish anyone at all, having heard Celsus speaking with exaggeration (δεινολογέω) and claiming that the writing entitled Disputation of Jason and Papiscus concerning Christ is worthy not of laughter but of hatred, to take into his hands the little writing (συγγραμμάτιον) and endure and bear to hear its contents, so that at once he may condemn (καταγιγνώσκω) Celsus, finding nothing worthy of hatred in the book. If someone reads (ἐντυγχάνω) impartially (ἀδεκάστως), he will find that the book does not even move to laughter; in which a Christian is recorded conversing (διαλέγομαι) with a Jew from the Jewish Scriptures and showing that the prophecies about the Christ fit (ἐφαρμόζω) Jesus, although the other, with the Jewish character (πρόσωπον), stands against the argument not ignobly (ἀγεννῶς) nor unfittingly (ἀπρεπῶς).
pass_b_english: Next after this, Celsus picks out, from all the writings that contain allegories and narratives in a style that is not to be despised, the humblest one, a work that can contribute something toward faith for the many and simpler people but is certainly not able to move the more intelligent. He says: “Such, for example, is a disputation between a certain Papiscus and Jason that I have come across, which deserves not laughter but rather pity and hatred. It is not my purpose, then, to refute these things; for they are plain to everyone, I suppose, especially if anyone will be patient and bear to listen to the writings themselves. I would rather teach the nature of things: that God made nothing mortal, but the works of God are all the things that are immortal, and mortal things are the works of those immortal beings. The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature. And in this respect the body of a bat, or of a maggot, or of a frog, will not differ at all from that of a human being; for the matter is the same, and what is perishable in them is alike.”

Nevertheless, I should like anyone whatever who has heard Celsus speaking so vehemently, and declaring that the writing entitled Disputation of Jason and Papiscus concerning Christ deserves not laughter but hatred, to take this little treatise in his hands and be patient and bear to listen to what is in it, so that he may condemn Celsus at once, since he will find nothing in the book that deserves hatred. If anyone reads it without prejudice, he will find that the book does not even move one to laughter. In it a Christian is recorded arguing with a Jew from the Jewish Scriptures and showing that the prophecies about the Christ fit Jesus; though the other, in the role of the Jew, holds his ground against the argument in a way that is neither ignoble nor unfitting.

choices.choice: τινός placed with Papiscus: 'a disputation between a certain Papiscus and Jason' (was 'a certain Disputation')
οἵαν δὴ καί: 'Such, for example, is'; ἔγνων 'I have come across'
πίστεως χάριν: 'contribute something toward faith for the many'
καίτοι γε clause: 'though the other, in the role of the Jew, holds his ground'; ἀπρεπῶς 'unfitting'
'immortal beings' remains an explanatory addition for ἐκείνων, flagged in notes

The copy-text has stray full stops (after συγγραμμάτων, ἐκείνων, πάνθ᾿ ὁντινοῦν, ἐντυγχάνῃ) that break single sentences; translated as continuous syntax. In Celsus's sentence τινός goes with Παπίσκου ('a certain Papiscus'), not with the disputation; ἔγνων rendered 'I have come across'. Celsus's 'mortal things are the works of those' (θνητὰ δ᾿ ἐκείνων): ἐκείνων most naturally refers back to the immortal works of God (the lesser gods of Plato, Timaeus 41a–d); 'immortal beings' is added to make the referent clear; compare Origen's own paraphrase in 4.54, 'the works of others'. ἐκεῖνο ... διδάξαι τὴν φύσιν is uncertain: 'teach the nature of things' (τὴν φύσιν as object) or 'teach this point about nature'. εὐλή is a maggot or worm. εὐτελέστερον 'the humblest/cheapest' (comparative used for the lowest of the set). Celsus quotes ἐλέους καὶ μίσους; Origen's restatement here gives only μίσους, kept so.
